item.title: [Field Level Media] Yordan Alvarez, Astros enter critical final stretch against Mariners

item.content:encoded:
Yordan Alvarez normally lets his bat do the talking.
But after the Houston Astros were swept in a three-game home series over the weekend by National League East champion Atlanta, Alvarez felt compelled to speak up at a players’ meeting.
“Basically for us, it was three slaps in the face they gave us right in front of our fans, especially,” Alvarez said through an interpreter. “Just use (Monday’s off day) to take it as a reset day and rest, and then the only thing left is to go out there and win the six games we have left.”
The Astros (77-79), who have lost 10 of their past 14 games, enter a two-game series Tuesday at Seattle one game behind Texas in the American League West race. They’ll complete the regular season with four games against the Athletics in West Sacramento, Calif.
Alvarez has held up his end of the bargain. The MVP front-runner leads the AL with a .313 batting average and ranks second in home runs (40) and RBIs (99) as he chases a Triple Crown.
Teammate Taylor Trammell said Alvarez’s words carried weight.
“He doesn’t talk much and when he speaks, there’s a presence,” Trammell said. “This was not a ‘hoorah’ or anything like that. It’s just like, ‘Hey guys, Easy. Just be easy with it,’ and hearing it from him, it means something. You see the way he’s played all year and you can’t tell me there hasn’t been any nicks or bangs for him. And he’s going out there every single day and being the best hitter in the game right now. That’s what he’s doing. And so when he says something and he talks, you listen.”
The Astros, who missed the playoffs on a tiebreaker last season to end an eight-year stretch of postseason appearances, hold the tiebreaker over Texas after winning the season series. The Rangers have three home games against the New York Mets and three games at Minnesota remaining.
The defending AL West champion Mariners (73-83) are five games behind Texas and dropped the season series to the Rangers, leaving them essentially one game from elimination.
They staved that off Sunday as rookie Kade Anderson pitched seven scoreless innings of three-hit ball, with no walks and seven strikeouts, in a 2-1 victory at Colorado.
“You just show up and … keep going,” Mariners catcher Cal Raleigh said. “That’s really all you can do. It’s frustrating, but we made our bed, and we’ve got to lay in it. And it’s our job to show up, play hard and put our best foot forward. It’s baseball, so you never know. Just keep fighting, keep battling, try to win one pitch at a time, and you know the rest is what it is.”
Tuesday’s series opener is set to feature a pair of right-handers, the Astros’ Cristian Javier (2-6, 5.31 ERA) and the Mariners’ Logan Gilbert (12-10, 3.69).
Javier suffered a 5-2 loss to visiting Kansas City last Wednesday, despite allowing just two runs over 5 1/3 innings. He’s 3-2 with a 2.87 ERA in nine career appearances against Seattle, including six starts.
Gilbert is coming off a 2-1 loss last Tuesday to the Angels in Anaheim, Calif., despite a quality start of six innings with two runs allowed. He’s 7-4 with a 3.18 ERA in 15 career starts against the Astros. Gilbert was the winning pitcher in a 6-1 victory April 12 in Seattle as he allowed one run on four hits over seven innings, with one walk and seven strikeouts.
–Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
These are the last MLB.com Power Rankings of the 2026 regular season. In exactly one week, 18 of these teams will go home, and 12 will be left. We have made it all the way through. Since these will be the final rankings, let’s take a look at each team, even the ones who did not make the playoffs, and find something positive its fanbase can feel about the 2026 season … now that it’s almost in the rearview mirror.
These rankings, as always, are compiled from MLB.com contributors whose names you can find at the bottom of this (and every) piece, but the words are mine. If you dislike the rankings, yell at all of us. But if you dislike the words, feel free to yell at me.
Also, as we close the season, we note for each team the highest they were ranked in our Power Rankings all season -- when they hit the peak.
1. Brewers (previously: 1)
Season High Water Mark: 1, this week
It’s the best season in Brewers history. It sure looks like they’re going to win 100 games for the first time ever. They’ve got a Cy Young frontrunner in Jacob Misiorowski, they’ve got all the momentum, and they’ve got a team that wins by doing all the little things right. Last year was a huge postseason bummer. Now is the time to right that wrong.
2. Dodgers (previously: 2)
Season High Water Mark: 1, Aug. 17
The Dodgers have had a lot of drama this year, much of it revolving around a hugely disappointing first season at Chavez Ravine for Kyle Tucker and injury concerns for Shohei Ohtani. And yet here they are, one of the best teams in baseball, as always, and the team everyone knows is looming in October.
3. Rays (previously: 4)
Season High Water Mark: 2, May 25
Don’t forget, almost no one picked the Rays to win the tough AL East this year. But it looks like it’s going to be theirs, with a deep, versatile roster led by Junior Caminero, who looks like he’s going to be a signature star in this league for the next decade-plus.
4. Braves (previously: 3)
Season High Water Mark: 1, June 15
Every year since their World Series title in 2021 has felt a little bit like a disappointment in its own way, even the 104-win season in '23. But this one sure hasn’t, with the Braves overcoming a '25 losing season by winning the division again. And check out Ronald Acuña Jr., who looks like a superstar again.
5. Yankees (previously: 5)
Season High Water Mark: 2, May 4
For a long time, it was assumed that if Aaron Judge was hurt for an extended period of time, the Yankees were cooked. But thanks to a fantastic pitching staff -- including Cy Young frontrunner Cam Schlittler -- the Yankees look as strong as ever. But it still may all ride on Judge regardless.
6. Cubs (previously: 6)
Season High Water Mark: 1, May 11
What more can you say about Pete Crow-Armstrong at this point? He’s about to end the Shohei Ohtani MVP reign, and he’s doing so while becoming one of the most popular players in the sport and having one of the best seasons in Cubs history. And it sure feels like October is going to fit him like a glove.
7. Red Sox (previously: 8)
Season High Water Mark: 6, Aug. 5
This season looked absolutely lost in June, and Red Sox fans were tearing their hair out. Then, suddenly, the Sox were playing the best of any team in baseball, and they rode that run all the way to a playoff spot. And it's sure looking like we'll get another installment of The Rivalry in the Wild Card.
8. Padres (previously: 9)
Season High Water Mark: 3, April 20
The Padres have justified all the investments A.J. Preller and company have made in the offseason with this late-season run, but they still have won just one game past the Division Series round this century. The top of the NL is tough this year, but no one’s hotter than the Padres.
9. Phillies (previously: 7)
Season High Water Mark: 5, July 16
It has been a rocky road, with Don Mattingly taking over early in the season, the team righting itself, and then struggling down the stretch. But in this ear, all that matters for the Phillies is the postseason. All of their questions are about to be answered, one way or the other.
10. Guardians (previously: 12)
Season High Water Mark: 5, June 8
The Guardians’ fight back to the top of the AL Central wasn’t as dramatic as last year’s, but if they can end up atop the division when it’s all said and done, it won’t matter. And if they do … they might just get a first-round bye out of it.
11. White Sox (previously: 11)
Season High Water Mark: 6, June 15
If the White Sox aren’t able to get into the playoffs after the fun season they’ve had, it will feel like a heartbreaker, but it probably shouldn’t be. This is a team that has lost 100-plus games for three consecutive seasons! Look at where they are now! The playoffs would be wonderful. But what a major step forward they’ve made. With more to come.
12. Rangers (previously: 16)
Season High Water Mark: 8, April 3
The Rangers have never gotten higher than three games over .500 this year … but that has not kept them out of the middle of the AL West, and even atop the division. They’ve only made the playoffs once in the last decade -- the year they won the World Series. That may well change this season.
13. Diamondbacks (previously: 10)
Season High Water Mark: 9, Aug. 17
The Padres’ torrid run down the stretch may end up keeping Arizona out of the playoffs, though the season’s final series between the two teams could have something to say about that. But a year of uncertainty ended up being a positive one, despite some off-field drama … and there’s still time left in this one.
14. Astros (previously: 13)
Season High Water Mark: 7, April 6
Yordan Alvarez had a fully healthy season and responded with an all-timer of an offensive performance. The only question now is whether they can catch the intrastate-rival Rangers for the AL West crown -- and it looks like they're going to have to, if they want to make the playoffs at all.
15. Blue Jays (previously: 14)
Season High Water Mark: 2, March 23
It looked for a while like the Jays, after the brutal way they lost the World Series last year, would make up for a disappointing season by sneaking into the final Wild Card spot. How fans feel about this season may depend on whether or not they can crawl their way back in. It’s going to be an uphill climb.
16. Pirates (previously: 15)
Season High Water Mark: 5, April 20
Pirates fans had big hopes for this year, and while they weren’t the playoff team that some had expected, they nevertheless have won 79 games and could notch their first winning season since 2018. It’s progress.
17. Orioles (previously: 19)
Season High Water Mark: 10, March 23
It may have hurt to do it, but the O’s did maximize their return for Adley Rutschman with even more young players to add to the ones they already have. It’s understandable if O’s fans are skeptical, but you can’t argue that Pete Alonso was a great investment, and really a North Star for the whole franchise at this point.
18. Marlins (previously: 18)
Season High Water Mark: 8, July 16
Take away that 12-game losing streak, and the Marlins are a playoff team this year. You obviously can’t do that, but the different way the Marlins have been doing things started to pay off this year. And they may well have a star in Otto Lopez.
19. Tigers (previously: 21)
Season High Water Mark: 8, April 27
This turned out to be their first losing season since 2023, which is frustrating because hopes were so high heading into the year, but there is still a ton of young talent here, led by Riley Greene, who is quietly putting together a stellar start to his career. And with the Tarik Skubal trade, there’s even more young talent on the way.
20. Cardinals (previously: 17)
Season High Water Mark: 8, May 18
The bullpen fell apart down the stretch, making the record look worse than the season felt, but the Cardinals made many steps forward this year, particularly with the lineup: Jordan Walker, JJ Wetherholt, Joshua Báez, Alec Burleson and Leo Bernal all look like lineup mainstays … with even more talent coming down the pipe.
21. Nationals (previously: 24)
Season High Water Mark: 12, June 22
James Wood is a star, but he was hardly the only National to emerge in 2026, with CJ Abrams and the recently extended Cade Cavalli setting themselves up as players the Nationals can build around. The offense was terrific this year: That’s the first time you’ve been able to say that in a long time.
22. Mariners (previously: 20)
Season High Water Mark: 3, March 23
So, yeah, it was a bit of a disaster season for the Mariners, in just about every possible way. But this was not a now-or-never season for the M’s: They have a very exciting rotation for 2027, and note that Cal Raleigh started to warm up as the season came to a close as well.
23. Mets (previously: 23)
Season High Water Mark: 5, March 23
That most of the offseason moves blew up in their faces is the reason they’re not in the playoffs, but they certainly played well enough in the second half to look like a playoff team, thanks largely to rookies Carson Benge, A.J. Ewing and Nolan McLean. The Mets will look different next year, but that’s a good thing.
24. Twins (previously: 22)
Season High Water Mark: 15, Aug. 5
The next generation of Twins stars has arrived: Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez all made their debut this year (and still have Rookie of the Year eligibility for next season). This was a transition year for the Twins. There’s plenty of reason to think they can turn the corner in 2027.
25. Reds (previously: 25)
Season High Water Mark: 6, April 27
This was the superstar step forward the Reds have been waiting for from Elly De La Cruz. They no longer have to wonder if he’s ever going to make the leap: He now has. And remember, he is still only 24 years old.
26. Royals (previously: 26)
Season High Water Mark: 14, May 11
Not much went the way it was supposed to this year, but there’s still a lot of young talent here. And there is Bobby Witt Jr., who, even in a down power year (for him), leads the American League in WAR, per FanGraphs.
27. Giants (previously: 27)
Season High Water Mark: 18, March 23
The terrible start, and the occasional discord and chaos, made this season feel like it was over with before it even began. But don’t overlook the fact that Rafael Devers, for most of this season, looked like the superstar the Giants traded for.
28. Angels (previously: 29)
Season High Water Mark: 19, April 20
A potential sale of the team is something that fans have wondered could change the trajectory of this franchise, and they’re going to get the opportunity to find out. There’s some young talent starting to percolate here, perhaps most notably Walbert Ureña, a 22-year-old who looks like he might already be an ace.
29. A’s (previously: 28)
Season High Water Mark: 10, May 11
The onslaught of injuries to their position players made people forget how good this lineup was at some point, and how late in the year they were in contention. As they move closer to their move to Las Vegas, there’s still plenty to build on here … and plenty of reason to have optimism for the future.
30. Rockies (previously: 30)
Season High Water Mark: 27, May 4
It does not look like the Rockies are going to avoid 100 losses this year, alas, marking four straight years with 100-plus losses. But they’ll still be double-digit games better than they were last year, and they’ll do so with a front office that seems, at last, to have a clear plan moving forward.
Voters: Jason Catania, Dan Cichalski, Theo DeRosa, Rick Gold Jr., Jared Greenspan, Will Leitch, Brent Maguire, Travis Miller, Brian Murphy, Arturo Pardavila, Shanthi Sepe-Chepuru, Andrew Simon, David Venn, Andy Werle.

item.title: [FanGraphs] Bobby Witt Jr. and the Off-Peak MVP Season
item.dc:creator: Davy Andrews
item.description: Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. item.content:encoded:
Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. A lower back injury in July will also limit him to a career low in games played. Put it together, and Witt is on pace to put up his the lowest WAR total since his 5.9-win 2023 campaign. Oh, and he also grabbed hold of the American League lead in WAR back in July and still hasn’t relinquished it. A down year by Bobby Witt Jr.’s standards is still good enough to make him a deserving MVP.
I don’t know if Witt is going to win his first MVP this year. Ours is the only flavor of WAR in which he leads the AL, and he leads by just a quarter of a win. He ranks third by Baseball Reference’s rWAR and is eighth by Baseball Prospectus’ WARP. Yordan Alvarez leads all of baseball in WARP because he’s hitting like, well, Yordan Alvarez and staying healthy like, well, someone other than Yordan Alvarez. Cam Schlittler leads the AL in Baseball Reference WAR, and he’s been so dominant that he deserves consideration for the Cy Young-MVP combo — if only he’d pitched just 23 fewer innings last year, he could’ve gone for the trifecta with Rookie of the Year. Kevin McGonigle has played like an MVP from the moment he arrived in Detroit, and Junior Caminero has surpassed 40 home runs for the second season in a row as a 23-year-old. All of these guys have a case, and they aren’t the only ones who merit inclusion in the discussion:
| Name | fWAR Rk | fWAR | rWAR Rk | rWAR | WARP Rk | WARP | Avg Rk | Avg WAR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bobby Witt Jr. | 1 | 6.6 | 3 | 6.5 | 8 | 5 | 4 | 6.0 |
| Yordan Alvarez | 2 | 6.4 | 4 | 6.4 | 1 | 7.3 | 2 | 6.7 |
| Cam Schlittler | 3 | 6.1 | 1 | 7 | 3 | 5.8 | 2 | 6.3 |
| Dylan Cease | 4 | 5.5 | 8 | 5.7 | 12 | 4.6 | 8 | 5.3 |
| Miguel Vargas | 5 | 5.2 | 10 | 5.3 | 2 | 5.9 | 6 | 5.5 |
| Junior Caminero | 6 | 5.2 | 7 | 5.7 | 5 | 5.3 | 6 | 5.4 |
| Kevin McGonigle | 7 | 5.1 | 2 | 6.7 | 4 | 5.3 | 4 | 5.7 |
| Randy Arozarena | 8 | 5.1 | 11 | 5.3 | 16 | 4 | 12 | 4.8 |
| Dillon Dingler | 9 | 4.6 | 25 | 4 | 23 | 3.3 | 19 | 4.0 |
| Drew Rasmussen | 10 | 4.6 | 21 | 4.2 | 13 | 4.4 | 15 | 4.4 |
| Reid Detmers | 11 | 4.6 | 35 | 3.7 | 11 | 4.7 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Parker Messick | 13 | 4.6 | 6 | 5.8 | 9 | 4.8 | 9 | 5.1 |
| Pete Alonso | 14 | 4.2 | 18 | 4.3 | 6 | 5.3 | 13 | 4.6 |
| Ceddanne Rafaela | 21 | 3.9 | 9 | 5.4 | 94 | 1.7 | 41 | 3.7 |
| Gavin Williams | 27 | 3.7 | 46 | 3.1 | 7 | 5.2 | 27 | 4.0 |
| Wilyer Abreu | 32 | 3.4 | 5 | 5.8 | 20 | 3.6 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Mike Trout | 40 | 3.2 | 28 | 3.9 | 10 | 4.8 | 26 | 4.0 |
Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jacob Misiorowski, Schlittler, McGonigle and JJ Wetherholt have made the AL MVP the only major award that’s really in question). If you want to read a particularly good example, you should check out the one Mario Delgado Genzor wrote for Baseball Prospectus on Friday. I want to focus on something slightly different — namely, how good Witt has already been in years when he missed out on an MVP and how unusual it would be for him to win it this year.
(A quick note before we get into it: We’re about to spend a lot of time talking about WAR. I know I mentioned rWAR and WARP earlier. They’re an important piece of the puzzle, especially due to the outsized effect rWAR in particular has on the MVP conversation, but from here on out, we’re sticking with good old FanGraphs WAR.)
This is Witt’s fifth major league season, and you could argue that it’s his fourth consecutive MVP-caliber campaign. Mind you, that argument would focus only on 2022, in which he put up 5.9 WAR, good for 10th in the majors. There’s no argument to be had about the 2024 and 2025 seasons. That said, along with Shohei Ohtani’s combined 9.2-WAR 2022 sesaon, they are the two most valuable seasons this decade for which a position player did not win an MVP. In 2024, Witt ran a 169 wRC+, stole 31 bases, and put up a Fielding Run Value of 11, fourth among all shortstops. That was good for 10.5 WAR, and it took the best season of Aaron Judge’s career – 58 home runs, a 19% walk rate, and a .322 batting average – to beat him. In 2025, Witt put up 8.0 WAR with a 130 wRC+, 38 steals, and 20 FRV, the best mark among all shortstops. Again, he was bested by a 10-win season from Judge and Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer campaign. Witt has never received a first place MVP vote.
Crow-Armstrong, who has the National League MVP all but locked down, gives us a great example of what it normally takes to win an MVP award. He may even finish with 10.5 WAR through his excellence in all three phases of the game, just like Witt did in 2024. Players like Judge, Ohtani, and Mike Trout, whose base level of talent is so high that a healthy campaign is almost sure to keep them a step above the rest of the league, don’t come around all that often. Even when they do come around, they still need to be playing at something close to their peak, and peaks don’t last that long. Until Ohtani, the only player to win more than three MVPs was Barry Bonds, whose regimen for raising and widening his peak has been well documented. Sometimes that’s because of voter fatigue, but often it’s because somebody else popped up with an amazing, undeniable season like PCA’s. Most of the time, the MVP is an already great player for whom everything goes perfectly. They stay healthy and they play not just their best, but over their heads. Think of Ronald Acuña Jr. winning the NL MVP in 2023 with 9.1 WAR, 4.1 more than his next-best total, or Mookie Betts winning the AL MVP in 2018 with 10.2 WAR, 2.8 more than his next-best total.
Generally speaking, since the voting started getting more rigorous in the last couple decades, those are the two categories of players who win MVPs. We see all-time greats who perform like only they are capable of performing, and we see excellent players who put it all together in a blaze of glory. Witt’s 2024 season probably falls into that second category. He wasn’t quite at his defensive or baserunning peak, but he put up his best season at the plate by nearly 40 points of wRC+ and DRC+, and he ended up with an all-timer of a season. His 10.5 WAR tied for the 36th-best position player campaign of all time. His company? Willie Mays and Babe Ruth twice apiece, Barry Bonds, and Rogers Hornsby. Unfortunately, he ran into one of those special players from the first category, in the form of Judge. If Witt had put up those 2024 numbers this year, he’d be en route to a unanimous MVP just like PCA.
But I said “in theory” earlier, and I said it because Witt isn’t done yet. He’s still just 26, and if not for those weeks he missed with back tightness, or a wOBA that’s more than 30 points below his xwOBA, he’d now be wrapping up his third straight seven-plus-win season. He’s elite in every facet of the game and he doesn’t look like he’s in danger of slowing down any time soon. It wouldn’t be much of a shock to see him rediscover his nine- or 10-win form. In other words, there’s at least a chance Witt belongs to that first category of player and not the second.
Earlier I mentioned Acuña and Betts claiming MVPs by putting up the best years of their careers by a long shot. That’s pretty standard. Especially in recent years, it’s awfully rare for a player to take home an MVP award in something other than the best season of their career, unless they also won the MVP in the best year of their career. Leaving those multi-time MVPs out (and excluding 2020 for obvious reasons), here’s the whole list of players who won an MVP in a year that wasn’t their best by fWAR since 2011: Giancarlo Stanton and Paul Goldschmidt.
Goldschmidt put up 6.8 WAR in his 2022 NL MVP season and 7.2 in 2015. In that sense, Goldschmidt fit a third archetype: the established star who doesn’t put up their biggest WAR total, and instead wins MVP as something of a career achievement award. Stanton put up 6.5 WAR in 2017, not quite the 6.8-win campaign he put up in 2014, but he was facing a weaker field, he was more established as a star, and he had the cachet of a 59-homer season. We’re talking about gaps of less than half a win. We had some multi-time winners, but Acuña, Betts, Cody Bellinger, Christian Yelich, Jose Altuve, Kris Bryant, Josh Donaldson, Andrew McCutchen, and Buster Posey all won MVP in the best seasons of their career by fWAR.
Let’s say that Witt does win the MVP this year. For the sake of round numbers, let’s say he closes strong and finishes with 7.0 WAR. That would be just the third-best season of his career, and a full 3.5 WAR below his career-high. Baseball Reference lists MVP winners going back to 1911, and in that time, Witt would become just the ninth position player to win MVP in a season that trailed their best year by such a wide margin. The list of players to do it before him is full of three-time MVPs like Joe DiMaggio, Mickey Mantle, and Mike Schmidt. Not only that, but you’ll note that if Witt does make this list, the only higher number in either column will belong to Mantle:
| Player | MVP Year | MVP WAR | Best Year | Best WAR | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frankie Frisch | 1931 | 4.1 | 1927 | 9.7 | 5.6 |
| Mickey Mantle | 1962 | 6.0 | 1956 | 11.5 | 5.5 |
| Willie Stargell | 1979 | 2.7 | 1971 | 8.2 | 5.4 |
| Joe DiMaggio | 1947 | 4.8 | 1941 | 9.7 | 4.9 |
| Freddie Freeman | 2020* | 3.0 | 2023 | 7.7 | 4.7 |
| Robin Yount | 1989 | 5.3 | 1982 | 9.8 | 4.5 |
| Andre Dawson | 1987 | 3.5 | 1982 | 7.3 | 3.8 |
| Mike Schmidt | 1986 | 5.8 | 1974 | 9.4 | 3.6 |
| Roger Peckinpaugh | 1925 | 2.4 | 1919 | 5.9 | 3.5 |
The last person to do so was Robin Yount, who won the AL MVP with 9.8 WAR in 1982, and then again with 5.3 WAR in 1989, long before anybody knew that Total Zone considered him the 11th-worst defender in the majors. This hasn’t happened in nearly 30 years, and Witt is in a very different boat here. He’s not one of the two MVP favorites because his season looks great to the eye but doesn’t fool the advanced metrics. He’s not an aging star who can count on some lifetime-achievement votes. He’s a young gun who’s leading his league in WAR because he excels in every facet of the game.
I realize that this is far from the most meticulous analysis I’ve ever conducted, and that MVP voting is and should be about more than WAR. Still, I hope I’ve put this season in the context it deserves. By our measuring stick, Witt has been the best player in the American League this season. He’s done so despite missing time due to injury. He’s done so despite some bad batted ball luck. And he’s done so despite not even coming close to the highest gear we know he’s got available to him, because that gear is so high that it’s normally reserved for inner-circle Hall of Famers. However the voting goes, Witt’s been in MVP form for three or four years now.
Davy Andrews is a Brooklyn-based musician and a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @davyandrewsdavy.bsky.social.

item.content:encoded:
Sure, the pennant race has taken centerstage the last few weeks, but soon enough 18 teams will start their offseasons earlier than expected. The Seattle Mariners, somehow, are one of those teams. It'll likely cost Dan Wilson his job, and force former AL Postseason heroes off the roster. But the Mariners aren't alone in terms of disappointing campaigns from contenders who made the postseason just a year ago. What of the Detroit Tigers, or even Cincinnati Reds in the National League?
In essence, that's what this time of the season is about for 18 teams. Looking back at what went wrong, and adjusting their offseason plans from there. Unfortunately for all of baseball, we're staring down the barrel at a lockout, which could force teams to rush their plans or miss out altogether, especially when it comes to Randy Arozarena, Brandon Lowe and Torey Lovullo.
Brandon Lowe wants to sign a new contract with the Pirates
Lowe had a series of walkoff hits this past week to prove his importance to the Pirates, even as Pittsburgh misses the postseason once again. The Pirates properly addressed their lineup this past winter, in part by trading for Lowe on an expiring contract. You could argue he's been their most consistent player, especially at the dish. Pairing Lowe, who is 32 years old, with Konnor Griffin for the next few seasons would show Pirates fans the front office and ownership is committed to winning for a change.
“I think this team’s got a very bright future and a lot of good players, and there’s a lot of good baseball that’s going to be played in this park for a long time. [If] they want to talk, I’m all ears," Lowe said on a possible extension.
Yet, Lowe could be a little out of the Pirates price range after the season he's had. Lowe 33 home runs and an .826 OPS in the middle of Pittsburgh's lineup. Considering just how thin the free-agent market is in terms of proven infielders — especially those who can hit at the level Lowe can — could make it tougher to meet his asking price.
Torey Lovullo knows this could be it with the Diamondbacks
The Diamondbacks August surge has turned into a September lull. The Diamondbacks remain alive in the NL Wild Card standings and face the San Diego Padres to end the season. Thus, if they can keep their deficit to three games or less, then perhaps the Snakes can fight for Torey Lovullo's job after all.
It's not as though Lovullo's message has grown stale in Arizona, but the way he dealt with the Ketel Marte drama lacked conviction. Eventually, all managers must move on the greener pastures, and Lovullo knows this.
“I understand it, it’s the realities of this game," Lovullo said, “and you got to win. That’s what it comes down to. I think we won a lot here. Have we won enough."
If Arizona can sneak into the playoffs, perhaps he can change his fate.
Could the Red Sox sign Randy Arozarena?
Arozarena is a free agent after the season and he's a fan favorite in Seattle. Despite Randy's World Baseball Classic kerfuffle with Cal Raleigh, the two seem to have a solid relationship at this point in the season. Arozarena rebounded and had a solid year, accruing a 5.3 bWAR and .861 OPS with 26 home runs as of this writing. Arozarena could be one of the best hitters on the open market. He's an above-average defensive outfielder, as well, with an arm we wouldn't recommend running on.
The 31-year-old was linked to the Boston Red Sox earlier this week by Ryan Divish, who is not a Boston sports media pawn, I can assure you. Still, the Red Sox have a lot of outfield depth as is, including in the farm system. Does it make sense to add Arozarena for a premium price?
For now, these are just rumblings. Arozarena can and should be connected to any number of teams this offseason, especiallty given the market lacks proven sluggers. Randy would be an upgrade for most teams, but the Mariners would be better off ponying up, barring there aren't any leftover issues between him and Raleigh.

item.content:encoded:
Cal Raleigh hit the longest home run of his MLB career in a loss against the Colorado Rockies, and MLB fans had a nuanced response.
The Seattle Mariners and Cal Raleigh have utterly failed to build upon the momentum of nearly making it to the World Series in the 2025 MLB season.
While they haven’t been mathematically eliminated yet, it is only a matter of time. ‘Big Dumper’ has been as disappointing as his teammates, although he did provide some entertainment on Saturday.
Raleigh slammed a gigantic home run, which was initially recorded as having gone 472 feet. It was later corrected, but at 459 feet, it is still the longest of his career.
MLB fans are in awe of Cal Raleigh’s hit but disappointed in him and the Seattle Mariners
In 2025, Cal Raleigh powered Seattle to a 90-72 season with 60 home runs and 125 RBIs, earning All-Star honours and finishing second in AL MVP voting.
In 2026, Raleigh’s production has fallen to a quite poor .184 average with 23 homers and 68 RBIs, while the Mariners sit at 72-83, all but guaranteed to miss the playoffs.
That’s what fans pointed to even as they were admiring the baseball star’s incredible home run hit.
“Well, about time he’s started back hitting home runs,” one fan said, their frustration clear. “Nice to see Cal is back, if only EVERYONE ELSE WAS BACK TOO,” another fan added.
“That is a meaningless HR, they have actually lost to the Rockies,” a third fan said. “Cal Raleigh, finally but too late to mean much for Seattle’s season,” a fourth fan claimed.
“If only we had this Cal earlier in the season – so many ‘what ifs’,” one Mariners fan lamented. “It has been a terrible season, but Cal Raleigh’s resurgence is a wonderful thing,” a sixth fan wrote.
It is bittersweet to see Raleigh finally playing at the highest level when the team’s season is all but over. However, a return to form bodes well for 2027, the Mariners and Raleigh will be raring to bounce back.

item.content:encoded:
The Mariners could enter this winter with a different starting shortstop and an opening in left field. Both big shoes to fill along with a much larger hole that would be hard to see on a depth chart. Randy Arozarena is headed toward free agency. J.P. Crawford’s contract also expires after the season. It’s likely that the Mariners move on from both, and if they do, the front office will spend plenty of time discussing alignments and where Colt Emerson fits.
They also will need to spend just as much time figuring out who takes over the room. Jon Morosi recently described the 2026 Mariners as the opposite of a cohesive team. We can debate how much clubhouse chemistry matters when the pitching regresses and prominent hitters underperform. Watching this season, it’s obvious Seattle did not look like a group pulling in the same direction.
Mariners Need a Clubhouse Successor Before Opening Day
The Mariners have spent years without steady clubhouse gravity. They’ve continuously churned through veterans. Carlos Santana arrived during the 2022 playoff push. Justin Turner filled the role in 2024. Eugenio Suárez brought his familiar energy back for the 2025 run. They find an established veteran, let him hang around just long enough to settle the room, then they begin their search for the next one.
That routine becomes dangerous when two of the most established players already inside the clubhouse are packing up and walking out together.
Arozarena was Seattle’s lone All-Star in 2026, plays with a pulse and has earned respect by posting up every day. We also watched another layer of his value emerge when Lazaro Montes reached the majors.
Montes spent his first series attached to Arozarena’s hip. There were jokes, celebrations and plenty of dugout energy, but there was also a veteran helping a 21-year-old navigate the largest jump of his career. Arozarena had become a mentor at exactly the moment Seattle’s next wave of young hitters began arriving.
The Mariners can decide his next contract will be too expensive, aging, diminishing defense, or how many outfielders they already have. They still have to replace what walks away with him.
Crawford presents a different version of the same problem. The Mariners have already paid Emerson like a central piece of their future, and the organization views him as Crawford’s successor at shortstop. That makes the transition fairly easy to see. The human transition is something else entirely.
Crawford has been with Seattle since 2019. He’s the longest-tenured Mariner and an established clubhouse leader who has lived through nearly every stage of this organization’s rebuild. He also welcomed Emerson rather than treating the highly paid prospect like an intruder coming after his job.
Emerson can inherit shortstop, but he won’t inherit the seven years of trust Crawford has built in Seattle. Say what you will about Crawford’s defensive lapses; he remains one of the biggest voices in the clubhouse. His name is often one of the first younger players mention when asked who helped them adjust, whether in the field or at the plate. Julio Rodríguez has even gone so far as to say that, among everyone on the roster, Crawford is the teammate he could most easily envision coaching in the majors one day. That’s not empty praise. Crawford carries real influence with his peers, and much of it goes unnoticed outside the clubhouse.
The Mariners will still have prominent voices. Cal Raleigh has become a face of the franchise. Josh Naylor carries himself like a veteran players naturally follow. Julio Rodríguez has reached the point where leadership comes with the size of his contract and stature.
That doesn’t remove Dan Wilson from the conversation, either. If the Mariners already had this many respected players and still struggled to establish a collective identity, the manager owns part of that failure. Adding a ceremonial clubhouse captain will not solve it.
The next veteran has to play and command respect without demanding attention. If they bring in a new face, he’ll have to connect Raleigh, Rodríguez and Naylor with Emerson, Montes, Michael Arroyo and the rest of the young guys arriving behind them.
Re-signing Arozarena would preserve one of those bridges. Bringing Crawford back in a reduced or evolving role could as well. Moving on from both remains a defensible baseball decision, provided the Mariners have an actual succession plan.
We have watched this organization act as though leadership can always be acquired at the last minute or at the trade deadline. The 2026 season exposed the flaw in that thinking.
If Arozarena and Crawford leave, Seattle cannot hand the clubhouse to whoever happens to have the most service time and hope a new identity forms by Opening Day. The Mariners need to know who takes over before the room becomes somebody else’s problem.
Tremayne Person is the Publisher for Mariners On SI and the Site Expert at Friars on Base, with additional bylines across FanSided’s MLB division. He founded the Keep It Electric podcast in 2023 and covers baseball with a blend of analysis, context, and a little well-timed side-eye just to keep things honest. Tremayne grew up a Mariners fan in Richmond, Va., and that passion ultimately led him to move to Seattle to cover the team closely and become a regular at home games. Through his writing, he connects with fans who want a deeper, more personal understanding of the game. When he’s not at T-Mobile Park, he’s with his dog, gaming, or finding the next storyline worth digging into.
